newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW-NZ non-bank lenders not a threat, yet.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-NZ non-bank lenders not a threat, yet.

text.p: Competition from non-bank New Zealand mortgage lenders had been given more credence than it deserved, but they were nevertheless acting to squeeze margins, ASB Bank Managing Director Ralph Norris said on Monday.
"The new entrants to the market have not taken very much market share at all," Norris said in an interview.
Norris said ASB's market share had increased over the last 12 months and had risen by 50 percent since 1992.
"So we have not seen any real impact on market share from the new entrants ... but they have obviously caused some acceleration in the contraction of margins," he said.
"The existing players are not sitting back and allowing business to be taken from under their noses and are obviously competing to obtain business," he said.
ASB's market share is around 14 percent. In its home city of Auckland, the share is around 35 percent. ASB is 75 percent owned by Commonwealth Bank of Australia
New Zealand's traditional mortgage lenders have recently faced competition from non-banks like Ergo, a telephone subsidiary of life insurer and pension fund AMP Society.
Norris said the lines between banks and insurers were going through a process of re-definition.

New entrants did not have to carry the baggage of branch networks and the high cost of transaction processing. "So therefore you have to reduce the cost transaction processing - using technology more effectively."
While many national banks are looking to rationalise their networks, ASB is the odd man out.

"We are going for a greenfields expansion approach. It has obviously been one that has been unusual," he said, adding buying other banks to acquire more "bricks and mortar" was not an appropriate model for the future.
"A lean and well-located branch network is much better than having a branch on every street corner," he said.
ASB had identified locations where it needed to have a presence with a view to establishing a "skeletal" network.

"A greenfields national expansion programme has been more cost-effective than some of the acquisition models that we have worked through," he said. ASB would be "fleshing out" its network over the next 12-18 months.
ASB did not enter a bid for Trust Bank New Zealand, which was taken over earlier this year by Westpac Banking Corp, because it did not fit with ASB's strategies.
"Basically, our view was that there were significant changes taking place, and will take place, over the next three-to-five years.
"We felt that as an organisation we could not afford to be diverted from the more strategic intitiatives that we are putting in place," he said.
Looking ahead, Norris said that with 80 percent of the New Zealand banking industry owned by Australian banks, much would depend on Australia's Wallis inquiry as to what happens domestically.
Commentators expect the inquiry to result in a wave of rationalisation in Australia's financial services industry.
-- Wellington Newsroom (64-4-4734746)
